                                Anatomy of the cranial nerves

  There are 12 pair of the cranial nerves, divided by their type into 3 groups:

  (1) Sensory: Olfactory, Optic, Vestibulocochlear
  (2) Motor: Oculomotor, Trochlear, Abducent, Accessory, Hypoglossal nerves
  (3) Mixed: Trigeminal, Facial, Glossopharyngeal, Vagus

lines: Anatomy of the cranial nerves
There are 12 pair of the cranial nerves, divided by their type into 3 groups:
(1) Sensory: Olfactory, Optic, Vestibulocochlear
(2) Motor: Oculomotor, Trochlear, Abducent, Accessory, Hypoglossal nerves
(3) Mixed: Trigeminal, Facial, Glossopharyngeal, Vagus
Cribriform plate of ethmoid bone: 1: Olfactory nerve
Optic canal: 2: Optic nerve
Superior orbital fissure: 3: Oculomotor nerve; 4: Trochlear nerve; 6: Abducent nerve; 5₁: branches of Ophthalmic nerve (lacrimal, frontal, nasociliary)
Foramen Rotundum: 5₂: Maxillary nerve
Foramen Ovale: 5₃: Mandibular nerve
Internal auditory meatus: 7: facial nerve; 8: vestibulo-cochlear nerve
Jugular foramen: 9: glossopharyngeal nerve; 10: vagus nerve; 11: accessory nerve
Hypoglossal canal: 12: Hypoglossal nerve
Foramen magnum
Foramen lacerum
Foramen spinosum
Cavernous sinus cross-section: lateral-wall nerves; ICA; SS; PG

 III. Oculomotor nerve: (motor + parasympathetic)

  - it emerges from the anterior surface of midbrain .
  - it then passes in the lateral wall of cavernous sinus
  - Here, it divides into a superior and an inferior division,
    which enter the orbital cavity through superior orbital fissure.












- The oculomotor nerve supplies the following :

  (a) all the extrinsic muscles of the eye except lateral rectus and superior oblique:
     - the superior branch supplies superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris.
     - the inferior branch supplies medial rectus, inferior rectus, inferior oblique

  (b) all the intrinsic muscles of the eye:
      - constrictor pupillae and the ciliary muscles (through ciliary ganglion)

 - Major functions of oculomotor nerve:
     (1) Regulating movements of upper eyelid and eyeball
     (2) Adjustment of lens for near vision, and constriction of pupil

 - Effect of lesion:
    (1) Ptosis. (due to denervation of levator palpebrae)
    (2) Internal ophthalmoplegia: Dilated, fixed pupil & Paralysis of accommodation
    (3) External ophthalmoplegia: Eye look down & out
    (4) Diplopia

   IV.  Trochlear nerve: (pure motor)
 - it is the smallest cranial nerve.
 - it is the only cranial nerve that orginates from posterior surface of brain stem
 - after it leaves posterior surface of the midbrain,
    it crosses to the opposite side,
  - it then passes in lateral wall of cavernous sinus
    and enters the orbit through superior orbital fissure.

 - The trochlear nerve supplies
    the superior oblique muscle of the eyeball .

- Effect of lesion:
    (1) difficulty in turning eye downwards
          and laterally
    (2) diplopia when looking downwards





 VI. Abducent nerve: (pure motor)

  - it emerges from the anterior surface of the brainstem
     between the pons and the medulla oblongata.
  - It passes forward with internal carotid artery through cavernous sinus
  - it enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.

  - it supplies the lateral rectus muscle, so it is responsible for turning eye laterally.

- Effect of lesion:
    (1) Internal strabismus
    (2) Diplopia when looking laterally

 V. Trigeminal nerve: (Mixed)

 - The trigeminal nerve is the largest cranial nerve .

 - it emerges from the anterior surface of the pons
    as a small motor root and a large sensory root.

 - The large sensory root expands to form the trigeminal ganglion .

 - it gives 3 main branches: ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular nerves


















(V1) Ophthalmic nerve: (sensory)

- It runs forward in lateral wall of the cavernous sinus
   and divides into 3 branches, the lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary nerves,
   which enter the orbital cavity through the superior orbital fissure .

(V2) Maxillary Nerve: (sensory)

 - it arises from the trigeminal ganglion
 - it passes forward in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus
    and leaves the skull through the foramen rotundum
    and crosses the pterygopalatine fossa
    to enter the orbit through inferior orbital fissure

 - it then continues as infraorbital nerve
    and it emerges on the face through the infraorbital foramen.

 - it gives sensory fibers to the skin of the face and the side of the nose .




















 Branches:
   From maxillary nerve:                              From infraorbital nerve:
    1) Ganglionic branches                                5) Middle superior alveolar nerve
    2) Zygomatic branch                                    6) Anterior superior alveolar nerve
    3) Meningeal branch                                    7) terminal branches
    4) Posterior superior alveolar nerve

   (V3) Mandibular nerve: (mixed)
 - it is the largest division of the trigeminal nerve
  - it is formed of a large sensory and a small motor root.
  - it passes out of the skull through the foramen ovale
  - The trunk then divides into a small anterior and a large posterior division.

  (A) Branches of Trunk:
      m 1- Nerve to medial pterygoid muscle: (supply tensor palati & tensor tympani)
       s 2- Nervous spinosus: (meningeal branch)

  (B) Branches from the anterior division:
     m 1- Muscular branches:  - To masseter, temporalis, lateral pterygoid
      S 2- Buccal nerve: - To cheek
               - it does not supply buccinator muscle which is supplied by the facial nerve

 (C) Branches from the posterior division:
       All of them are sensory except mylohyoid nerve.

     (1) Auriculo-temporal nerve:
          - it carries parasympathetic supply to the parotid salivary gland.

     (2) Lingual nerve:
        - it is joined by chorda tympani nerve
        - lingual nerve carries general sensation from anterior 2/3 of tongue
        - chorda tympani nerve carries taste sensation from anterior 2/3 of tongue

    (3)  Inferior alveolar nerve:
       - it enters mandibular foramen and passes through the mandibular canal
          to supply teeth of lower jaw
       - it divides into: incisive and mental branches.
       - Before entering the canal, it gives off mylohyoid nerve,
           which supplies mylohyoid muscle and anterior belly of digastric muscle


- Effect of Trigeminal Nerve Lesion:

   (1) Loss of general sensation (hemianesthesia) from face and oral & nasal cavities

   (2) Loss of corneal reflex (V1)

   (3) Paralysis of the muscles of mastication

   (4) Deviation of the mandible to the weak side

   (5) Paralysis of the tensor tympani muscle:
          Leads to partial deafness to low-pitched sounds

   (6) Trigeminal neuralgia






.

 VII. Facial nerve: (mixed)

 - it has a large motor root and a small sensory component.

 - it emerges from anterior surface of brainstem
    between the pons and the medulla oblongata .

 - it passes with vestibulocochlear nerve in the cerebellopontine angle
   to enter the internal acoustic meatus

   - then, it enters facial canal and expands to form the sensory geniculate ganglion .
 - finally, it emerges through stylomastoid foramen to enter the parotid gland
   where it gives off its terminal branches that pass to the muscles of face and scalp

- Branches of the facial nerve :

  (1) Greater petrosal nerve:
     - it passes through the pterygoid canal to reach the pterygopalatine ganglion
       to give parasympathetic supply to lacrimal gland, glands of nose and palate.

   (2) Nerve to stapedius: - supplies the stapedius muscle in the middle ear.

   (3) Chorda tympani:
       - it joins the lingual nerve to the anterior 2/3 of the tongue for taste sensation

       - it passes to the submandibular ganglion
         to give parasympathetic supply to submandibular & sublingual salivary glands

   (4) Nerve to posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid muscle

   (5) Posterior auricular nerve: - to occipitalis muscle

   (6) Five terminal branches: - to the muscles of facial expression.
     - These are temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular, and cervical branches .


  - Lesion of facial Nerve:

    (1) the face appears emotionless and expressionless on the paralyzed side
           due to paralysis of facial expression muscles.

    (2) Loss of corneal reflex

    (3) Loss of taste from the anterior ⅔ of tongue

    (4) Decreased salivation

   (5) Deviation of angle of mouth toward healthy side
        (due to traction of the muscles toward the healthy side).

 - In case of Upper motor neuron lesion:
      - only the lower half of face is affected

 - In case of Lower motor neuron lesion: (as Bell’s palsy)
      - the upper and the lower halves of the face are paralyzed.

 VIII.   Vestibulocochlear nerve: (sensory)
  - it is a sensory nerve that consists of vestibular and cochlear parts.
  - They leave anterior surface of brainstem between pons and medulla oblongata.
  - it enters the internal acoustic meatus with facial nerve.

 (1) Vestibular fibers:
     - The vestibular fibers originate from the vestibule and the semicircular canals;
                          Vestibular ganglia
     - they are concerned with sense of position of head and equilibrium
     - Effect of Lesion: results in disequilibrium, vertigo, nystagmus, ataxia

 (2) Cochlear fibers:
     - The cochlear fibers originate in spiral organ of Corti in the cochlea
                            spiral ganglion of the cochlea.
     - they are concerned with hearing
     - Effect of Lesion: deafness or tinnitus

IX. Glossopharyngeal nerve: (mixed)

- it emerges from the anterior surface of medulla oblongata
   between the olive and inferior cerebellar peduncle.

 - it leaves the skull by passing through the jugular foramen.

- Branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve: (Ph TMLC)

   (1) Pharyngeal branches: run to the pharyngeal plexus .

   (2) Tympanic branch:
           tympanic plexus      lesser superficial petrosal nerve         otic ganglion
            auriculotemporal nerve         parasympathetic supply to parotid gland

    (3) Muscular branch:
      - to stylopharyngeus muscle .

    (5) Lingual branch:
      - to the posterior third
        of the tongue .

    (5) Carotid branch:
         - to the carotid sinus






   - Lesion of glossopharyngeal nerve (IX):
       (1)  Loss of gag reflex (afferent limb)
   (2) Hypersensitive carotid sinus reflex (syncope)

   (3) Loss of general sensation in the oropharynx

   (4) Loss of taste from posterior ⅓ of the tongue

   (5) Glossopharyngeal neuralgia

 X. Vagus nerve : (mixed)

- it emerges from the anterior surface of the medulla oblongata
    between the olive and the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

 - it leaves the skull through the jugular foramen .

       - the cranial root of accessory nerve joins the vagus nerve
           and is distributed mainly in its pharyngeal and laryngeal branches
           for supply of all muscles of pharynx (except stylopharyngeus),
           larynx and palate (except tensor palati)


 - Branches of vagus nerve:

 (1) Meningeal branch:
 (2) auricular branch:
 (3) Pharyngeal branch:

 (4) Recurrent laryngeal nerve:
        - left recurrent laryngeal nerve
           it hooks around arch of aorta
        - right recurrent laryngeal nerve
            hooks around subclavian artery

 (5) Superior laryngeal nerve:
         - it divides into the internal
            and the external laryngeal nerves.

 (6) Cardiac branches:

 - lesion of Vagus nerve:

   (1) Ipsilateral paralysis of the muscles of the soft palate, pharynx, larynx.
          Leading to dysphonia, dyspnea, dysarthria& dysphagia

  (3) Anesthesia of pharynx & larynx

  (2) Loss of gag reflex

XI. Accessory nerve: (motor)

- It consists of cranial and spinal roots:

 - Cranial root:
    - it emerges from the anterior surface of the medulla oblongata
       between the Olive and the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
            - innervates muscles of palate, larynx and pharynx (important for swallowing)
 - Spinal root:
    - it arises from the upper 5 cervical segments
       of the spinal cord.
    - it enters the skull through foramen magnum.
       to join the cranial root,
       then they leave skull through jugular foramen.

  - The spinal root innervates sternomastoid
      and trapezius muscle .
     (important for head and shoulder movement)

     - Effect of Lesion:
       (1) Difficulty in moving the head
        (2) Shoulder drop


 XII. Hypoglossal nerve: (motor)

 - It emerges on anterior surface of the medulla oblongata
    between the pyramid and the olive

 - it leaves the skull through the hypoglossal canal.

 - it gives muscular branches to tongue muscles

   - Effect of Lesion:
      - deviation of the tongue to the affected side when protruded
        (due to paralysis of genioglossus muscle)

lines: Cranial nerves & Nuclei - summary table
I Olfactory - Sensory (SVA). Smell. Openings in cribriform plate of ethmoid.
II Optic - Sensory (SSA). Vision. Optic canal.
III Oculomotor - Motor (GSE, GVE). Raises upper eyelid, turns eyeball upward, downward, and medially; constricts pupil; accommodates eye. Superior orbital fissure.
IV Trochlear - Motor (GSE). Assists in turning eyeball downward and laterally. Superior orbital fissure.
V Trigeminal - Ophthalmic division: Sensory (GSA). Cornea, skin of forehead, scalp, eyelids, and nose; also mucous membrane of paranasal sinuses and nasal cavity. Superior orbital fissure.
Maxillary division: Sensory (GSA). Skin of face over maxilla; teeth of upper jaw; mucous membrane of nose, the maxillary sinus, and palate. Foramen rotundum.
Mandibular division: Motor (SVE). Muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor veli palatini, and tensor of tympani. Foramen ovale.
Mandibular division: Sensory (GSA). Skin of cheek, skin over mandible and side of head, teeth of lower jaw and temporomandibular joint, mucous membrane of mouth and anterior part of tongue.
VI Abducent - Motor (GSE). Lateral rectus muscle turns eyeball laterally. Superior orbital fissure.
pages.transcription: Visually transcribed row-by-row from the embedded summary table. Source wording is retained; corrections are separate reference notes.

lines: VII Facial - Motor (SVE). Muscles of face and scalp, stapedius muscle, posterior belly of digastric, and stylohyoid muscles. Internal acoustic meatus, facial canal, stylomastoid foramen.
Sensory (SVA). Taste from anterior two thirds of tongue, from floor of mouth and palate.
Secretomotor (GVE) parasympathetic. Submandibular and sublingual salivary glands, the lacrimal gland, and glands of nose and palate.
VIII Vestibulocochlear - Vestibular: Sensory (SSA). From utricle and saccule and semicircular canals - position and movement of head. Internal acoustic meatus.
Cochlear: Sensory (SSA). Organ of Corti - hearing.
IX Glossopharyngeal - Motor (SVE). Stylopharyngeus muscle - assists swallowing. Jugular foramen.
Secretomotor (GVE) parasympathetic. Parotid salivary gland.
Sensory (GVA, SVA, GSA). General sensation and taste from posterior one third of tongue and pharynx; carotid sinus (baroreceptor); and carotid body (chemoreceptor).

X Vagus - Motor (GVE, SVE). Sensory (GVA, SVA, GSA). Heart and great thoracic blood vessels; larynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs; alimentary tract from pharynx to splenic flexure of colon; liver, kidneys, and pancreas. Jugular foramen.

XI Accessory - Cranial root: Motor (SVE). Muscles of soft palate (except tensor veli palatini), pharynx (except stylopharyngeus), and larynx (except cricothyroid) in branches of vagus. Jugular foramen.
Spinal root: Motor (SVE). Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
XII Hypoglossal - Motor (GVE). Muscles of tongue (except palatoglossus) controlling its shape and movement. Hypoglossal canal.
